hints: Look closely at the AB row in the table. What antibodies does a person with blood group AB have in their plasma?
Remember the transfusion rule given: agglutination happens only if the recipient's antibody matches the donor's A or B antigen. If the recipient has no antibodies, which donor antigens are safe?
walkthrough:
**Check the recipient**

Look at the AB row in the table. A person with group AB has both A and B antigens on their red cells, but has neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies in their plasma.

This is the key clue. No antibodies means nothing to attack donor cells.

**Apply the transfusion rule**

The question tells us a transfusion is unsafe only if the recipient has antibodies to the donor's antigens.

Since the AB recipient has no anti-A and no anti-B, they cannot react against A antigens or B antigens from a donor.

**Test all donor groups**

Donor A brings A antigen: safe, no anti-B problem because AB has no anti-B. Donor B brings B antigen: safe, no anti-A problem. Donor AB brings A and B: safe. Donor O brings neither antigen: safe.

So an AB person can receive from A, B, AB and O. This is why AB is called the universal recipient.

options.A: Too restrictive. AB can receive AB blood, but because they have no antibodies they can also safely receive other groups.
options.B: Too restrictive. Group O has no antigens so it is safe, but groups A, B and AB are also safe for an AB recipient.
options.C: Incomplete. A and B are safe, but AB and O are also safe because the AB recipient has no antibodies to react with them.
options.D: Correct. An AB recipient has neither anti-A nor anti-B, so no donor A or B antigen will be attacked. All four groups can be given.
